inputs.text:
I just heard about this ruling from the Punjab and Haryana High Court under Justice Sumeet Goel. They made it clear that anticipatory bail can't be yanked away simply because stolen articles weren't recovered from a house or because the allegations sound serious on their own. Cancellation only sticks if there's solid evidence of the person misusing their liberty or some other major new development, and the court turned down the push to revoke the pre-arrest bail in this case.

Despite some trying to frame this as a win for the accused at the expense of victims and accountability, it's really the same old tactic to put unproven claims and so-called social order ahead of real safeguards. What this highlights is how the justice system gets weaponized against vulnerable people through heavy allegations that lack any backing to prove actual misuse. By insisting on concrete proof instead of letting technicalities or vague fears drive cancellations, the court is pushing back against patterns of inequality where institutions protect existing power rather than examining who gets hurt most by rushed enforcement. This matters deeply for protecting those who face systemic disadvantages, as it stops the legal process from becoming another tool to reinforce historical imbalances, discipline the marginalized, and shield the structures that benefit the few.
